title: Critical path analysis
examples: How do I draw the activity network correctly?
What exactly is the float value telling me?
Can you show me an example with more than three activities?

explain.say: Today we learn about critical path analysis. This helps plan projects efficiently. We use activity networks to map tasks.
An activity network shows tasks and their order. Arrows show which task must finish first. Think of building a simple model.
The earliest start time is the soonest a task can begin. It depends on the finish time of its predecessors. This sets the minimum schedule.
The float is how much a task can delay without delaying the project. It is the difference between latest and earliest times. This gives flexibility.
The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent tasks. Any delay here delays the entire project completion. These tasks have zero float.

faq.q: What is the difference between the earliest and latest times?
faq.a: The earliest time is the soonest a task can possibly start or finish. The latest time is the last it can start or finish without issues.
asks: What is the latest allowable time?

faq.q: If a task has zero float, what does that mean for the project?
faq.a: It means the task must start and finish exactly on schedule. Any delay to this task delays the whole project.
asks: Does zero float mean it's critical?

faq.q: Do I need to calculate the critical path for every single project?
faq.a: No, you calculate it when you need to manage time constraints. It helps find the project's minimum completion time.
asks: When should I use this method?
Is this only for building projects?

faq.q: How do I know which tasks are dependent on each other?
faq.a: The activity network diagram shows these dependencies using arrows. An arrow from A to B means B needs A to finish first.
asks: How do I map out the sequence?

faq.q: Is the critical path always the longest path?
faq.a: Yes, by definition, the critical path represents the longest sequence of dependent activities. This sets the minimum project duration.
asks: Is it always the longest path?

facts: The critical path determines the shortest possible time to complete a project.
Float represents the amount of time a task can be delayed without delaying the project end date.
Tasks on the critical path have a float value of zero.
The earliest finish time of a task is its earliest start time plus its duration.

quiz.say: If Task A finishes at time five, what is the earliest start time for Task B that follows it?
quiz.why: The earliest start time for Task B must be at least the time Task A finishes.

wrong.0: This ignores the dependency; Task B cannot start before Task A finishes.
wrong.1: This assumes a fixed gap, which is incorrect for dependency scheduling.
wrong.2: This calculates the finish time, not the start time.

quiz.say: A task has an earliest time of three and a latest time of five. What is its float?
quiz.why: Float is the difference between the latest time and the earliest time, so five minus three is two.

wrong.0: This only uses the latest time, ignoring the earliest time constraint.
wrong.2: This incorrectly adds the two times together.
wrong.3: This only uses the earliest time, ignoring the latest time constraint.

quiz.say: In a sequence A $\rightarrow$ B $\rightarrow$ C, if A is critical, which statement must be true?

options.show: Task C must have zero float
options.say: Task C must have zero float

options.show: The total project time is unknown
options.say: The total project time is unknown

options.show: Float for Task A is zero
options.say: Float for Task A is zero

options.show: Task B must also be critical
options.say: Task B must also be critical

quiz.why: If a task is on the critical path, it has no slack, meaning its float must be zero.

wrong.0: The critical path must be checked end-to-end, not just based on the first task.
wrong.1: Knowing one critical task helps determine the overall minimum project time.
wrong.3: While often true, Task B could have float if Task C is very short.
